strengths: Timely identification of real DoS vulnerability in deployed MoE systems with clear practical implications for infrastructure providers
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 14 popular models and 139 HuggingFace models with multiple evaluation metrics (coverage, system-level latency, API latency)
Well-motivated theoretical framework: TMI formula correctly characterizes maximum imbalance with elegant regime analysis for sparse vs. dense models
Black-box attack requiring no gradient access or optimization, with model-agnostic applicability using simple repetitive token patterns
Novel side-channel finding that latency amplification patterns can infer backend model architecture and approximate deployment scale
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-defined threat model and methodology
Length scalability analysis (Fig. 6) demonstrates robustness across prompt lengths and system prompts, suggesting fundamental vulnerability rather than narrow edge case
weaknesses: Overstated universality claims: Abstract states 'nearly all models susceptible' but Table 3 shows significant variation (Mixtral 2.5-2.9× vs. Qwen3/GPT-OSS 1.01-1.35× at EP=8); sparser models exhibit substantially lower vulnerability, contradicting generality narrative

Shallow mechanistic understanding: Paper asserts embeddings are 'immediately dominated' by repetition but provides no ablation studies, dimension-wise analysis, or theoretical justification for why routers fail under repetitive inputs

Limited practical impact: Simple perplexity filtering (PPL~1 vs ~5) is highly effective and easily deployable; paper acknowledges no commercial APIs currently use it but doesn't evaluate robustness against mixed-pattern variants

Ethical concerns inadequately addressed: No clear evidence of responsible disclosure to affected service providers (ChatGPT, DeepSeek); side-channel architecture inference on commercial systems raises consent questions
Coverage metric (Eq. 4) measures theoretical concentration under worst-case GPU assignment but disconnects from actual latency; unclear how coverage of 0.6 maps to specific LAR values

Side-channel architecture inference claims are speculative: Inferring EP size from latency ratio lacks rigorous validation; other deployment factors (batching, dynamic reallocation, hardware heterogeneity) could produce similar latency patterns

Incomplete defense evaluation: Perplexity filtering tested only at extremes (PPL~1 vs ~5); Algorithm 1 evaluated via simulation only, not on deployed systems; no analysis of compatibility with existing load balancers (EPLB)
Limited technical novelty: Core attack is simply token repetition; the vulnerability is an artifact of EP architecture rather than a novel attack methodology requiring sophisticated design
Missing ablation studies: No analysis of partially repetitive tokens, sensitivity to different token patterns, or comparison with other input perturbations

Insufficient depth on router training: Does the auxiliary loss used in training inadvertently create the vulnerability? Could better-designed balance losses prevent imbalance under adversarial inputs?

strengths: Identifies a timely and previously undocumented vulnerability in widely-deployed MoE models with comprehensive empirical evaluation across 14 models and multiple metrics
Black-box attack method is simple and practical, requiring no gradient access or architectural knowledge
Well-executed experiments with clear methodology, proper controls, and testing across varying EP sizes and commercial APIs
Systematic investigation of 139 HuggingFace models and extended analysis of length scalability, vulnerable expert distributions, and side-channel effects
Addresses an important practical concern as MoE models see rapid commercial deployment (DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, etc.)
weaknesses: Limited understanding of root cause: the mechanism (repetitive tokens → similar embeddings → identical routing) is straightforward; no causal analysis of why routers fail or how to fundamentally fix this at the architecture level
Unclear practical impact: evaluation uses individual requests without considering realistic batching in modern inference systems, which would likely mitigate latency amplification significantly
Overstated DoS claims: demonstrates latency amplification for single requests, not true denial of service impact on batched systems or typical serving workloads

Proposed defenses are ineffective: perplexity filtering requires overhead and isn't deployed in practice; vulnerability-aware load balancing shows only modest gains (8-36%) and is configuration-dependent
Shallow theoretical contribution: TMI formula (Eq. 3) is trivial combinatorics without revealing insights; missing analysis of router training dynamics or learned behaviors
Limited evaluation of commercial deployments: only 3 ChatGPT variants tested for latency amplification; insufficient to characterize real-world impact
Sparse model performance undermines broad vulnerability claims: for increasingly-popular sparse models (Qwen3-Next, DeepSeek-V2), latency amplification is only 1.3-1.6× even at EP=8
No novel algorithmic or methodological contributions: attack is trivial (token repetition); defenses are standard techniques (perplexity filtering, load balancing) with limited effectiveness
Missing ablation studies: unclear what token diversity is needed to avoid concentration, which features trigger vulnerability, or how other routing mechanisms would respond
Side-channel analysis (Section 4.3) is underdeveloped with only 3 API samples and speculative claims about ChatGPT's architecture without rigorous validation

strengths: Identifies timely and practical vulnerability in widely deployed MoE systems with comprehensive empirical evidence across 139 models and 14 detailed evaluations
Simple yet effective black-box attack requiring no gradient access; elegantly demonstrates fundamental weakness in MoE router behavior
Solid theoretical analysis with Theoretical Maximum Imbalance (TMI) formula providing principled bounds on attack severity under different sparsity regimes
Real-world validation on commercial APIs (Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen, DeepSeek, ChatGPT) demonstrating 1.5-4.7× latency amplification with practical impact
Thorough extended analysis including length scalability (Section 5.1), vulnerable expert distribution patterns (Section 5.2), and side-channel implications
Clear presentation with effective visualizations; responsible disclosure with ethical statement and defense proposals
weaknesses: Root cause analysis lacks depth: while demonstrating that repetitive tokens cause imbalance, the paper provides only superficial explanation of why MoE routers trained with load-balancing constraints remain vulnerable to OOD patterns

Defense proposals are incomplete and ineffective: perplexity filtering adds overhead and isn't deployed; vulnerability-aware load balancing reduces coverage by only 10-36% and works in limited configurations; neither addresses fundamental router vulnerability

Limited scope of deep API testing: extensive real-world latency evaluation (Table 4) focuses primarily on Mixtral-8x7B; no systematic investigation of how batching, deployment configurations, and concurrent requests affect attack effectiveness

Simulation-reality gap: coverage metric B relies on router output simulation without full system execution; batching, KV caching, and dynamic scheduling effects on bottleneck manifestation are not empirically validated

Speculative explanations without verification: Section 5.2's hypothesis about intermediate experts as 'fallback mechanisms' lacks validation; sparse expert vulnerability pattern deserves deeper investigation
Threat model incompleteness: no analysis of API rate limits and costs, cascading effects with multiple concurrent requests, or budget constraints on realistic attacks

strengths: Novel identification of routing imbalance as a weaponizable DoS vector in MoE systems; first work to demonstrate this threat distinct from prior resource exhaustion attacks

Comprehensive experimental validation across 139 MoE configurations with 13 representative models; thorough evaluation from multiple perspectives (cross-vocabulary, cross-model, latency impact, Expert-GPU mapping effects)
Strong theoretical foundation with clear mathematical characterization (Eq. 3-5) of embedding variance minimization objective and theoretical maximum imbalance bounds
Black-box attack requiring no knowledge of model parameters or routing mechanisms; practical demonstration on commercial LLM APIs showing 1.5-4.7× TTFT amplification
Real-world impact quantification including SLA violation analysis; demonstrates P99 degradation from 99% to 86.4% under realistic conditions
Transparent and honest discussion of practical limitations (Section 4.4, 5.4) including Expert-GPU mapping uncertainty and constraints on attack performance
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, well-organized research questions, high-quality figures (especially Figures 1, 3, 4), and accessible writing
Extended robustness analysis (Section 6.1) showing vulnerability persists across prompt lengths and system prompts; systemic nature of the architectural flaw
weaknesses: Critical gap between claimed universality and practical impact: Expert-GPU mapping is unknown in black-box settings, causing actual TTFT degradation to vary dramatically (1.22× to 2.48×) depending on unknown deployment details; Figure 3 demonstrates routing concentration doesn't guarantee GPU bottleneck

Theoretical-empirical connection incompletely justified: claim that token repetition solves the embedding variance minimization objective (Eq. 4) is empirically motivated but lacks formal proof of how layer-wise attention, position encoding, and normalization affect this assumption

Real-world DoS effectiveness underspecified: paper evaluates impact within batches or at low request rates (minute-wise for APIs) but doesn't quantify attack intensity (α) needed for SLA violations at operational request rates or total system throughput degradation at scale

Insufficient exploration of defenses: PPL-based filtering shows clear detection capability (Table 6: attack PPL ~1 vs natural text ~10-75) but dismissed as impractical without empirical overhead measurement; vulnerability-aware Expert placement achieves up to 36.7% reduction but dismissed too quickly

SLA analysis assumptions not fully validated: Log-Normal distribution parameters derived from aggregate request distributions; O(N) prefill complexity claim for Qwen3-30B-A3B needs broader validation; distribution shape parameter invariance claim needs clarification
KV caching bypass claim (Section 4.2) stated but not experimentally validated despite being presented as important to attack robustness

Reproducibility limitations: no code release announced; commercial API experiments irreproducible; vocabulary scanning process could be more precisely specified; some models have restricted availability
Responsible disclosure details missing: no specification of vendor contact, embargo periods, or specific mitigations recommended to system providers before public release
Missing ablation studies: which tokens are most effective? sensitivity to prompt structure? expected success rates given mapping uncertainty? detection difficulty measurements

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 139 MoE models on HuggingFace with systematic testing of 13 representative architectures across multiple EP sizes (2-256), providing broad evidence of vulnerability universality

Well-structured experimental methodology addressing three clear research questions (RQ1-3) with appropriate metrics (bottleneck coverage, LAR) that quantify attack impact on realistic metrics (TTFT, SLA violations)

Practical demonstration of real latency impact with GPU profiling showing 1.29× to 2.48× TTFT increases and quantified SLA degradation (P99 → P86.4), supported by both local experiments and commercial API testing

Honest acknowledgment of fundamental constraints on attack performance (unknown Expert-GPU mappings, inability to control target experts) with theoretical analysis of upper bounds (TMI metric in Eq. 5)
Clear presentation of core vulnerability with effective visualizations (Figures 1-3) illustrating the straggler bottleneck mechanism; well-organized paper structure with informative appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty of attack mechanism: the core contribution (using repetitive tokens to concentrate routing) is trivially simple and represents a straightforward consequence of feeding homogeneous embeddings to a router, rather than a sophisticated attack or fundamental insight

Fundamental practical limitation inadequately addressed: attack effectiveness is highly probabilistic when Expert-GPU mappings are unknown, contradicting the 'black-box' framing—Section 4.4 acknowledges this but the limitation severely constrains real-world weaponizability

Weak real-world validation: most experiments use local vLLM deployments on controlled infrastructure; API testing (Table 3) involves only 8 commercial services at minute-wise intervals with sparse temporal coverage, insufficient to demonstrate systematic SLA violations in production systems

No defense mechanisms proposed: while the paper identifies the problem, it offers no novel solutions and dismisses practical defenses (perplexity filtering showing PPL≈1.1 vs. natural text PPL≈9-76) as impractical without convincingly addressing why a threshold-based filter wouldn't work

Technical concerns with SLA analysis (Appendix B): the Log-Normal distribution analysis assumes uniform LAR scaling and σ invariance under linear scaling, but ignores fixed latency overhead; SLA predictions are highly sensitive to distribution parameter assumptions with limited robustness analysis

Insufficient depth on architectural understanding: while the paper documents that repetitive tokens cause concentration, it provides limited insight into *why* routers are susceptible (e.g., Figure 6 shows layering patterns without explanation); the connection between minimizing embedding variance (Eq. 4) and routing concentration lacks rigorous proof

Measurement gaps and limited generalization: batch size is fixed at 16,384 tokens; experiments use only prefill-decoding disaggregation strategy; Figure 6 analysis (layer-wise concentration patterns) lacks mechanistic explanation; only 13 models explicitly tested despite claiming 139-model universality

Incomplete threat model and cost analysis: no per-token cost-benefit analysis for API attacks; unclear how minute-wise API testing captures realistic attack patterns; no comparison with other MoE deployment strategies that might be more robust

Problematic terminology and framing: calling this a 'denial-of-service' attack is misleading (system remains available, only degraded); claims of universality are overstated given the probabilistic nature under unknown deployments; 'black-box' claim is weakened by vocabulary scanning requirements

strengths: Identifies and comprehensively demonstrates a critical system-level vulnerability in widely-deployed MoE inference systems with expert parallelism, showing real-world impact through both local experiments and commercial API evaluations

Achieves universal vulnerability assessment across 139 HuggingFace models and 13 selected models, with systematic evaluation of multiple dimensions (EP sizes 2-256, model families, attention mechanisms, sparsity levels)

Provides strong theoretical foundation through embedding variance characterization (Eq. 3-4) and Theoretical Maximum Imbalance (TMI) analysis that elegantly captures how deployment constraints limit attack effectiveness

Rigorous experimental methodology with well-designed metrics (bottleneck coverage, LAR_moe, LAR_ttft), proper statistical reporting with confidence intervals, and thorough SLA impact analysis using Log-Normal distribution modeling

Black-box attack design requiring no model access makes the vulnerability practically relevant; demonstrated effectiveness on commercial APIs with 1.5×-4.7× latency amplification shows real-world applicability

Excellent presentation with clear figures (especially Figures 1, 3, 6), logical flow through three well-motivated research questions, and honest discussion of attack constraints and defense limitations
weaknesses: Limited proposed solutions undermine practical impact: vulnerability-aware load balancing (Algorithm 1) only provides conditional mitigation failing for high EP sizes and sparse models; generic recommendation to 'limit EP size' is often infeasible; no novel inference-time defense mechanisms proposed

Threat model assumptions reduce scope: requires attackers and victims in same batch (somewhat artificial), assumes static Expert-GPU mapping within relocation windows, and API experiments conducted at low request rate to avoid service disruption—unclear if findings hold under sustained attacks

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: limited justification for L2 embedding variance choice (Eq. 3), minimal ablation studies (only repetitive tokens tested; mixed patterns, repetition frequencies unexplored), and core insight (repetitive tokens→similar embeddings→same routing) is relatively straightforward once identified

Restricted experimental scope: evaluated only on A800 GPUs (generalization to H100/TPUs unclear), single batch size of 16,384 tokens, single inference engine (vLLM only), no evaluation against models already using inference-time load balancing, limiting reproducibility and generalization

Weak RQ3 defense evaluation: vulnerability-aware mapping tested under oracle conditions where defenders know vulnerable experts; true black-box defense scenario (attacker unaware of mapping AND defender lacking prior vulnerability knowledge) underspecified; effective expert metric (Eq. 8) indirect and not directly validated

Missing exploration of fundamental defenses: no investigation of batch-level defenses (request scheduling, selective isolation), minimal discussion of inference-time load balancing strategies despite acknowledging gap, dismissal of perplexity filtering lacks empirical baseline, no proposed principled defense architecture

Reproducibility gaps: exact system prompts unspecified, ShareGPT selection criteria unclear, GPU memory configurations undocumented, code availability unmentioned; jump from theoretical objective (Eq. 4) to repetitive tokens approximation lacks rigorous justification

Limited analysis of generalization: routers with auxiliary inference-time load balancing not evaluated, autoregressive generation effects on routing consistency unexplored, alternative routing strategies (top-2, GShard variants) not tested, interaction with dynamic EPLB evaluated only briefly in appendix
